title: MODULE 02 — HTTP Protocol and API Design

overview.text: Module objective: Understand how applications communicate through HTTP, how APIs expose application functionality, and how to design consistent, secure, scalable, and well-documented APIs.
In Module 01, you learned how backend applications are structured and how a request travels through a backend.
In this module, you will go deeper into the communication layer.

You will learn how to design APIs that frontend developers, mobile applications, other backend services, and external integrations can consume without needing to understand the internal implementation of your backend.
A student opens a course, requests its modules, opens a lesson, marks the lesson complete, and checks their progress.

Behind these actions, the frontend communicates with different API endpoints. Each endpoint needs a well-defined method, URL, request format, response format, status code, permissions, and error-handling behavior.
This module teaches you how to design that complete communication contract.

blocks.text: API stands for Application Programming Interface.
An API is a defined interface through which one software application or component communicates with another.
It specifies what operations are available, what information must be provided, and what results can be returned.
A customer does not enter the kitchen and directly access the ingredients, equipment, or cooking process.
The customer looks at the menu.
The restaurant returns the prepared food.
The frontend does not need direct access to the backend's internal functions, database tables, or source code. It sends a request through a defined interface, and the backend processes it.
The client communicates through the API, not through direct access to private backend internals.
Imagine building a learning platform with:
All these applications may need the same student information and course data.
Without a shared backend interface, developers might implement the same business logic separately in multiple applications.
Different applications may calculate progress differently.
Each application may implement its own permissions.
Security rules may differ between clients.
An API provides a shared interface.
React Frontend | Android App | iOS App | Instructor Dashboard | v Shared API | v Backend Services | v Database
All clients use the same backend rules and data access policies.
Suppose a student wants to see their enrolled courses.
The API receives the request and passes it to the appropriate backend handler.
The frontend reads the JSON and displays the courses.
The frontend does not need to know whether the backend uses PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, or another database.
It only needs to understand the API contract.
APIs are not limited to websites or HTTP.
Client-defined data queries through a typed schema
Functions exposed by a software library
Interfaces provided by an operating system
Interface for querying and managing data
An API describes an interface. REST, GraphQL, and gRPC are different approaches to designing or implementing communication interfaces.
A professional API should have the following qualities.
Consistency: Similar operations follow similar naming and response conventions.
Predictability: Developers can understand how an endpoint behaves without guessing.
Security: Requests are authenticated and authorized where necessary.
Validation: Invalid data is rejected with useful error information.
Documentation: Developers can discover endpoints, inputs, outputs, and limitations.
Maintainability: Changes can be introduced without unnecessarily breaking existing clients.
Performance: Responses are designed to avoid unnecessary data transfer and processing.
Reliability: The API handles expected failures and unexpected conditions gracefully.
1.6 API vs endpoint vs API request
These terms are related but not identical.
API: The complete interface offered by a software system.
Endpoint: A particular network address and operation exposed through an API.
API request: An individual call made to an endpoint.
API: Course Management API Endpoint: GET /api/v1/courses Request: GET /api/v1/courses?category=backend
One API can contain hundreds of endpoints. Each endpoint may support different HTTP methods.
APIs can also be classified by their intended consumers.
Public API: An API made available to external developers or customers, often with registration, documentation, and usage restrictions.
Private API: An API intended for internal applications and services within an organization.
Partner API: An API made available to approved external organizations through controlled access.
A learning platform's internal progress API may be private.
Its instructor integration API may be a partner API.
A public course catalog API may be available to external developers.
A public API does not mean unauthenticated or unrestricted access. Public APIs often require credentials, rate limits, and usage policies.

HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
It is an application-level protocol used for communication between clients and servers.
HTTP defines how requests are constructed, how responses are returned, and what common elements such as methods, status codes, and headers mean.
The current core HTTP semantics are specified in RFC 9110.
A typical HTTP exchange involves two messages:
HTTP request: Sent by the client.
HTTP response: Sent by the server.
GET /api/v1/courses HTTP/1.1 Host: api.prepspaces.com Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
An HTTP request generally contains the following components:

POST /api/v1/courses HTTP/1.1 Host: api.prepspaces.com Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Accept: application/json { "title": "Backend Engineering", "description": "Learn backend development" }
Identifies the resource or target of the request.
Identifies the HTTP message version in this illustrative HTTP/1.1 request.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use different wire formats, but preserve the core HTTP request and response semantics.
Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Accept: application/json
Headers communicate metadata about the request.
The body contains the information submitted to the backend.
Not every request has a body. A GET request, for example, normally retrieves information without requiring a request body.
Optional reason phrase in protocol representations such as HTTP/1.1.
HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json Location: /api/v1/courses/course-101 { "success": true, "data": { "id": "course-101", "title": "Backend Engineering" } }
Status code: 201 indicates that a resource was created.
Response headers: Describe the response, such as its content type and resource location.
Response body: Contains the created course information.

Step 1 — Client action: The administrator submits a course creation form.
Step 2 — Request construction: The frontend builds an HTTP POST request.
Step 3 — Network transmission: The request travels to the backend.
Step 4 — Authentication: The backend validates the administrator's identity.
Step 5 — Authorization: The backend verifies that the administrator can create courses.
Step 6 — Validation: The server validates the submitted course information.
Step 7 — Business logic: The course service executes the creation rules.
Step 8 — Persistence: The database stores the new course.
Step 9 — Response: The backend returns 201 Created with the created resource representation.
Step 10 — UI update: The frontend displays the newly created course.
In a typical synchronous HTTP interaction, the client sends a request and waits for the response to that operation.
async function getCourses() { const response = await fetch( "/api/v1/courses" ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error( `HTTP error: ${response.status}` ); } return response.json(); }
The await keyword means that the function waits for the asynchronous operation to complete before proceeding.
However, the browser can still perform other work while the network operation is pending.
It is important to distinguish synchronous API semantics from blocking the entire browser or server process.
HTTP has evolved to improve communication efficiency and performance.
Early HTTP; commonly opened separate connections for individual requests
Persistent connections, standardized host handling, and other improvements
Binary framing, multiplexed streams, and header compression
HTTP semantics over QUIC, using UDP as its transport foundation
HTTP/1.1: Supports persistent connections, allowing connections to be reused rather than reopened for every request.
HTTP/2: Supports multiplexing multiple streams over a single connection and compresses headers using HPACK.
HTTP/3: Uses QUIC and improves transport behavior, including reducing certain head-of-line blocking problems associated with TCP.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not fundamentally change what GET, POST, and status codes mean. They primarily improve the transport and messaging mechanisms.
HTTP is designed as a stateless protocol.
This means each request's meaning can be understood independently; HTTP does not automatically remember that a user successfully logged in during a previous request.
The student then makes another request:
The second request still needs valid authentication information, such as a session cookie or bearer token.
The backend uses that credential to establish the student's identity.
Stateless protocol design does not mean that applications cannot maintain user sessions, shopping carts, progress, or other information.
It means that such application state must be handled through explicit mechanisms rather than being assumed from the previous HTTP request.
A common misunderstanding is that every HTTP request requires a completely new network connection.
HTTP/2 can multiplex independent streams on one connection.
These mechanisms reduce unnecessary connection overhead and improve communication efficiency.
These concepts are important when building reliable APIs.
Safe method: A method is safe when its defined semantics are essentially read-only; it is not intended to request a change to server state.
Idempotent method: A method is idempotent when multiple identical requests have the same intended effect on server state as one request.
This is generally idempotent because repeatedly replacing the same resource representation should produce the same intended state.
This is generally neither safe nor inherently idempotent because repeated requests may create multiple resources.
Suppose a frontend sends a payment request, but the network connection fails before the response arrives.
The client cannot necessarily know whether the backend completed the payment.
Blindly sending the same request again could result in a duplicate charge.
For operations that must prevent duplicate effects, APIs can implement idempotency keys:
The backend tracks the key and ensures that repeated submissions of the same operation do not create duplicate effects within the defined idempotency window.
Idempotency is especially important for payments, enrollment operations, order creation, and other sensitive mutations.

sections.title: 3. HTTP Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE

blocks.text: HTTP methods communicate the intended operation that a client wants to perform on a resource.
For example, a course management application may need to:
Instead of inventing a different URL for every operation, HTTP provides standardized methods.
The method and target resource together establish the semantics of the request.
GET is used to retrieve a representation of a resource.
A GET request is defined as a safe and idempotent method.
The server should not perform an application-state modification merely because a client requested the resource.
GET requests should generally not be used for creating or modifying resources.
3.3 POST — Create resources or execute operations
POST requests ask the server to perform resource-specific processing on the submitted request content.
A common use is creating a new resource.
The server creates the course and returns its identifier.
POST can also be used for operations such as:
This creates an enrollment resource associated with the course.
POST is not automatically idempotent. If a client repeats a creation request, duplicate resources may be created unless the API has a duplicate-prevention strategy.
PUT requests are used to create or replace the state of the target resource, according to the API's resource model.
{ "title": "Advanced Backend Engineering", "description": "A complete backend development program", "status": "published" }
The server applies the submitted representation as the replacement representation according to its contract.
{ "success": true, "data": { "id": "course-101", "title": "Advanced Backend Engineering", "description": "A complete backend development program", "status": "published" } }
A PUT request is defined as idempotent.
A repeated identical PUT should produce the same intended resource state.
Important: PUT should not silently behave like a partial update unless that is explicitly the resource's documented design. For partial modification, PATCH is generally the clearer choice.
PUT can also create a resource at a client-selected URI when the API supports that behavior.
PATCH is used to apply partial modifications to a resource.
Suppose a course has these attributes:
An administrator only wants to change its status.
PATCH is not inherently idempotent. Its behavior depends on the patch instructions.
For example, an operation that increments a counter by one would produce a different result each time it is repeated.
One common patch format is JSON Merge Patch. With that format, null can be used to remove a field, so the API must define its null-handling rules carefully.
DELETE requests ask the server to remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality or representation, according to the resource's semantics.
The course is deleted or otherwise removed according to the API's documented lifecycle.
Some applications use soft deletion instead of physically deleting records.
In such an application, DELETE may move a resource into a deleted or archived state rather than immediately erasing its database record. The contract should explain the behavior.

DELETE is an idempotent HTTP method in terms of its intended effect. This does not require every repeated request to return an identical status code. For example, the first request may return 204 and a later one may return 404.
CRUD is an application-level concept. HTTP methods are protocol-level mechanisms. They are related, but not exactly the same thing.
Mistake 1: Using GET to modify data
Why it is wrong: GET is a safe retrieval method. Automated systems, crawlers, and caches may issue GET requests in contexts where they do not expect state changes.
Mistake 2: Using POST for every operation
This creates inconsistent HTTP semantics and makes caching, tooling, and client expectations less predictable.
Prefer resource-oriented URLs and appropriate HTTP methods.
Mistake 3: Treating PATCH like full replacement
If the client sends only a status field, the backend should not accidentally delete other fields simply because they were absent from the request.
Define PUT and PATCH behavior clearly.
Mistake 4: Assuming PUT and POST are interchangeable
PUT has replacement semantics and idempotency guarantees; POST has resource-specific processing semantics.
Choose based on the intended operation.
Choose the correct HTTP method for each operation:
Change only a student's phone number
Retry a payment without creating a duplicate charge
Expected answers: GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE, GET, POST, and POST with a suitable idempotency mechanism.

4.1 What is an HTTP status code?
An HTTP status code is a three-digit number returned by the server to indicate the result of processing a request.
Indicates that the requested resource could not be found.
Status codes are grouped into five categories.
Request or client-side condition caused a problem
Server failed to fulfill a valid request
Used when a request is successfully completed and a response representation is normally returned.
Used when the request successfully creates a resource.
The response may include a Location header containing the URI of the new resource.
Indicates that the request has been accepted for processing, but processing has not necessarily completed.
Example: a large report-generation job is queued.
Indicates that the request was successfully processed and there is no response content.
Commonly used after a successful DELETE or certain update operations.
Used when the server returns a requested partial representation, commonly for range requests.
The resource has a new permanent URI.
Indicates that a cached representation can still be used under the relevant conditional request.
For example, a browser may send an If-None-Match header and receive 304 when its cached resource is still current.
PATCH is not supported for that resource
Server cannot provide an acceptable representation
Validly structured request violates validation rules
Server does not support the requested method or functionality
Upstream service did not respond in time
A status code should reflect what actually happened. Do not return 200 when a database operation failed, simply because the server was able to produce a JSON response.
These three codes are particularly important in secure API design.
The client has not provided valid authentication information.
No valid session or token is provided.
The client is authenticated but does not have permission to perform the operation.
A student attempts to delete an administrative resource.
The requested resource does not exist, or the API chooses not to disclose its existence to an unauthorized requester.
A secure application may deliberately return 404 instead of 403 for certain private resources to reduce information disclosure.
HTTP headers are metadata fields included in requests and responses.
Headers are separate from the response body.
GET /api/v1/courses HTTP/1.1 Host: api.prepspaces.com Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Here, Accept and Authorization are request headers.
Identifies the intended host in HTTP/1.1
Indicates the message content length where applicable
Identifies the origin of a browser request
Makes a request conditional on a matching entity tag
Makes a request conditional on an entity tag not matching
Describes the response body media type
Identifies a created resource or redirection target
Indicates the modification time of a resource
Provides guidance on when to retry
Lists supported methods for a resource
These two headers are easy to confuse.
Content-Type: What format is being sent?
Accept: What format does the client want to receive?
The client wants a JSON response.
A server may return 415 Unsupported Media Type when the submitted media type is unsupported.
It may return 406 Not Acceptable when it cannot provide an acceptable response representation.
The backend validates the supplied credential and establishes the authenticated user's identity.
A bearer token must be protected. Never include real tokens in screenshots, public logs, source control, or documentation examples.
For browser applications, cookie-based sessions are also common. When cookies are used for authentication, appropriate Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, and CSRF protections must be considered.

Suppose a course catalog does not change frequently.

sections.title: 5. Request Parameters, Query Parameters and Request Bodies

blocks.text: An API endpoint defines an operation, but the backend often needs additional information to understand what the client wants.
But what happens when the frontend wants:
Courses created by a particular instructor?
The API needs a way to receive these values.
HTTP APIs commonly use path parameters, query parameters, headers, and request bodies.
Path parameters identify a particular resource or one of its nested resources.
The backend uses these values to identify the requested resources.

app.get("/api/v1/courses/:courseId", async (req, res) => { const courseId = req.params.courseId; const course = await courseService.findById(courseId); if (!course) { return res.status(404).json({ success: false, message: "Course not found" }); } res.status(200).json({ success: true, data: course }); });
retrieves the value from the URL path.
When to use path parameters: Use them when the value identifies the resource or resource hierarchy being accessed.
Query parameters provide additional instructions for retrieving or processing resources.
They appear after a question mark (?) in the URL.
A query string can contain multiple parameters:
This might request Java-related courses ordered by creation time, newest first.
The exact meaning of the parameters must be documented.
When to use query parameters: Use them for filtering, sorting, searching, pagination, and optional retrieval preferences.
A request body contains data submitted by the client.
It is commonly used with POST, PUT, and PATCH.
The backend reads the JSON body and validates it before processing the request.

app.use(express.json()); app.post("/api/v1/courses", async (req, res) => { const { title, description, category, difficulty } = req.body; if (!title || !description) { return res.status(400).json({ success: false, message: "Title and description are required" }); } const course = await courseService.create({ title, description, category, difficulty }); res.status(201).json({ success: true, data: course }); });
The example demonstrates basic validation. A production implementation should additionally use a dedicated validation schema and centralized error handling.
Meaning: Retrieve courses matching the backend category.
Meaning: Create a course with the supplied information.
5.6 A complete example combining all three
Suppose an administrator wants to update a particular course.
PATCH /api/v1/courses/course-101?notifyStudents=true Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Content-Type: application/json { "title": "Advanced Backend Engineering", "status": "published" }
notifyStudents=true is a query parameter controlling an optional behavior.
The JSON body contains the changes.
